headline: France’s Bookstores, Beloved Curators of Literature, Are in a Deep Crisis

paragraphs.text: When old friends and loyal customers gathered for a book club in Strasbourg, France, last month, the only thing missing was the books. The group met in an empty room that had housed one of the city’s most beloved bookstores, Dinali, before it closed its doors this summer after 54 years.

“It’ll take some time before I can fully come to terms with it,” said Jennifer Goepp, who had owned the store with her husband, Thierry, and was welcoming the book club members to what was left of it.

The Goepps are not alone. Last year, 85 bookstores went out of business in France. It was the first year in recent history that the country had seen more bookstores close than open. Earlier this year, Gibert Joseph, France’s largest independent bookstore chain, founded in 1888, filed for bankruptcy protection.

“We’re drowning right now,” said Alexandra Charroin Spangenberg, the head of the national booksellers’ union. “If we lose the network of independent bookstores,” she said, “we lose part of France’s cultural identity.”

With more than 3,200 shops, France has one of the most deeply rooted bookstore cultures in the world, surviving a broader shift to online book-buying better than many places. The United States, with nearly five times the population, has only about 500 more bookshops. Bookstores help give French literature its idiosyncratic character by giving shelf space to aspiring writers whose work might be overlooked in mass-market online book selling.

Being an independent bookseller — a “libraire,” as the French call it — is not like any other retail job. People can study the trade at universities and earn a widely respected diploma. “I think of it as a calling rather than a job,” said Ms. Charroin Spangenberg, who owns a bookstore in St.-Étienne, a town in central France.

Yet France leaves its libraires little room to absorb rising costs. They run an average profit margin of 1 percent, making them among the country’s least profitable retailers, according to the booksellers’ union.
“A baker, when the price of butter and flour goes up, simply raises the price of his baguette,” Mr. Goepp said. “We can’t.”

That’s because, under a 1981 law named after Jack Lang, the culture minister at the time, publishers fix book prices nationwide. The main purpose is to protect small bookshops from predatory discounting by large retail chains. But the law leaves booksellers with little flexibility to set their own prices. By September, retail prices overall were up more than 3 percent from a year earlier, but book prices rose only about 1 percent.

Shops like Dinali must also compete with the likes of Amazon. Over the years, the Lang law was amended to limit the sway of online sellers — fixing e-book prices and restricting deals on delivery fees — but their selection and fast delivery still give them an edge over bricks-and-mortar stores.

“I buy online when I can’t find what I need in a bookstore,” said Hugo Muré, 22, a law student who shopped at Dinali. Mr. Muré said he often needed titles that arrived much faster online, adding: “I can’t afford to wait.”
The post-pandemic boom, when shoppers rallied to support independent businesses, has long faded. Shops like Dinali have recorded a near 14 percent drop in sales since 2021, according to the union.

These pressures eroded Dinali’s profit margins until there was no choice but to shut down. After running a deficit for three years, Mr. Goepp said he and his wife made the decision to close all three Dinali stores in Strasbourg in late 2025.
“We realized that the next step would mean cutting staff positions,” said Ms. Goepp, who added that would have hurt their ability to curate their shelves thoughtfully.

Sophie Noël, a sociologist at Panthéon-Assas University in Paris, said, “These bookstores really give a voice to, and provide opportunities for, books that would never be able to gain traction through other channels.”
“Take Samuel Beckett,” she said.

The Nobel-winning Beckett was born in Dublin but lived most of his life in France, frequently writing in French. Still, he initially had little commercial success there. Between the spring of 1947 and the summer of 1948, he sold exactly four copies of his novel “Murphy.” The risk taken by small bookstores to keep stocking him allowed him to slowly build a readership in a way that helped sustain his career, particularly until his play “Waiting for Godot” brought him global acclaim.

Customers said they were drawn to Dinali by its distinctive selection, and mourned the loss like a death in the Strasbourg community. For Françoise Houari, 58, a longtime customer, the book club helped cushion the blow.

At last month’s meeting, about a dozen members perched on plastic chairs, amid ripped-out floorboards, presenting the books they had chosen. Ms. Houari brought a “mendiant,” a traditional Alsatian cake made from stale brioche, alongside her choice of book, Douce Dibondo’s “Le Mouvement.” Mr. Goepp chose a pastry recipe book, a nod to the new career he is starting at 63.

The Goepps have turned the store’s old main space, on a cobblestone street with half-timbered houses in Strasbourg’s old town, into a chocolate store and cafe. It has an upstairs reading space, where they display the old Dinali sign on a shelf, flanked by books.
Ms. Charroin Spangenberg, the union head, is less hopeful about the future. “We’re going to have to get through this crisis,” she said, “and our concern is how many of us will survive.”
